title: Checkpoint: Castles and Knights
objective: After this level you can explain how land, castles and knights held medieval society together.
summary: Medieval bishops described society as those who pray, fight and work. A timeline from the first castles to the plate revolution, plus five questions, ties land, castles and knights together.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: a medieval bishop sorted society into three kinds of people.
cards.body: Those who pray, those who fight and those who work. You’ve just spent a chapter with two of them. Let’s put land, castles and knights on one page.

events.label: Castles begin to spread across western Europe
Henry I gives Geoffrey of Anjou a shield of golden lions
King John’s miners bring down a corner of Rochester’s keep
A revolution from mail to plate armour

cards.headline: Pray, fight, work
cards.body: In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Like chivalry, it was an ideal, but a medieval one, unlike the modern pyramid. It maps this chapter well. Many knights held land as fiefs and fought for their lords. Serfs worked the lord’s demesne every week. And castles, the homes of kings and lords, held the land together. Fighters, workers, and the stone that kept them in place.

mascot.line: Land, castles, knights and forty very unlucky pigs. That’s a chapter well earned.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How land for service tied lords, vassals and knights together, and why historians question feudalism.
What a serf owed his lord, from weekly work on the lord's land to fees for marrying and dying.
How castles grew from earth mounds into layered stone, and why most sieges ended by hunger or treachery.
Where the ideal of chivalry parted from how knights really fought and whom they chose to spare.

questions.prompt: Castles and knights: which order of events is right?

options.label: Geoffrey’s lion shield, the siege of Rochester, the plate revolution
The siege of Rochester, Geoffrey’s lion shield, the plate revolution
The plate revolution, Geoffrey’s lion shield, the siege of Rochester
options.rationale: The plate revolution came last, from 1325.

options.label: Geoffrey’s lion shield, the plate revolution, the siege of Rochester

questions.prompt: Castles and Knights recap: what did a medieval serf need his lord’s permission for?

options.label: To go to church on Sundays
To marry, leave his village or change his work
To grow any crops at all
To speak to other serfs
options.rationale: Not a rule on the manor.

questions.explanation: A serf could not permanently leave, marry or change his occupation without his lord’s permission.

questions.prompt: How did the idea of three orders differ from the feudal pyramid?

options.label: It came from kings; the pyramid came from peasants
options.rationale: Bishops wrote of three orders; the pyramid is modern.

options.label: It left out knights; the pyramid included them
options.rationale: Those who fight are one of the three orders.

options.label: Medieval bishops described it; the pyramid is a modern model
It had five orders; the pyramid had three

questions.explanation: Bishops like Adalbero of Laon described three orders; the pyramid is a later simplification.

questions.prompt: Castles and Knights recap: what was a gatehouse portcullis?

options.label: A tunnel dug under the gate
A tower on wheels for attackers
An opening for pouring hot sand
A heavy grille dropped to seal the gate

questions.explanation: A portcullis was a heavy wooden or iron grille that could drop to seal the gate passage.

questions.prompt: Castles and knights: why did a king grant land for knight service instead of paying wages?

options.label: Knights were forbidden to handle coins
A knight’s armour and horse were costly to buy and keep
Land was worthless in the Middle Ages
options.rationale: Land was the main source of wealth.

options.label: The Church paid knights’ wages instead
options.rationale: The land came from the king.

questions.explanation: A knight had to buy his own costly equipment; land held for service helped pay for armour and horses.
